subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science Reading - Atoms, Elements and Compounds
subtitle: Reading passages for KS3 chemistry classification, formulae, separation and evidence questions.
description: These short KS3 chemistry passages build reading fluency around atoms, elements, compounds, mixtures, formulae, the periodic table and working scientifically. Questions mix fact retrieval, inference, data interpretation and explanation.

data.sourcePassage: Chemistry studies substances: what they are made from, how they behave and how they can change. All matter is made from tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are far too small to see with the naked eye or with ordinary school microscopes, so scientists use models to represent them. A simple particle diagram may show atoms as circles or letters, but it is not a real picture and it is not drawn to scale. The model is useful because it can show whether particles are all the same or different, whether atoms are joined, and whether a substance is an element, compound or mixture. At KS3, students also use a simple atomic model: a tiny nucleus contains protons and neutrons, while electrons are found around the outside. Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge and electrons are negative.

questions.question: Why do scientists use models for atoms?
questions.modelAnswer: Atoms are too small to observe directly with ordinary school equipment, so models help scientists represent and explain them.

questions.question: Which particle has a positive charge?
questions.modelAnswer: A proton has a positive charge.

questions.question: What does a particle diagram help a student decide?
questions.modelAnswer: It helps decide whether particles are the same or different, whether atoms are joined, and whether the substance is an element, compound or mixture.

questions.question: Why is an atom diagram called a model rather than a real picture?
questions.modelAnswer: It is simplified and not drawn to scale; real atoms do not look exactly like the diagram.

questions.question: Explain one limitation of the simple atom model described in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: It does not show the true scale of the nucleus compared with the atom or how electrons really behave.

data.sourcePassage: An element is a pure substance made from only one type of atom. Copper, oxygen, carbon, iron and helium are elements. Some elements exist as single atoms, such as helium gas, while others are often found as molecules. Oxygen gas is O2, which means two oxygen atoms are joined together. It is still an element because only oxygen atoms are present. A compound is different: it contains atoms of two or more different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Water is H2O, so each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Carbon dioxide is CO2, so it contains one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. A molecule is any group of atoms chemically joined, so a molecule is not always a compound.

questions.question: Which substance in the passage is an element made from single atoms?
questions.modelAnswer: Helium gas is an element made from separate helium atoms.

questions.question: What does O2 show?
questions.modelAnswer: O2 shows two oxygen atoms joined together.

questions.question: Why is O2 not a compound?
questions.modelAnswer: It contains only oxygen atoms, so only one type of atom is present.

questions.question: How many hydrogen and oxygen atoms are shown in H2O?
questions.modelAnswer: H2O shows two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.question: Explain why the statement "every molecule is a compound" is wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: A molecule is atoms joined together, but it can be made from one element, such as O2; a compound must contain different elements.

data.sourcePassage: A mixture contains two or more substances that are together but not chemically joined into one fixed substance. The substances in a mixture often keep many of their own properties and they are not present in one fixed ratio. Air is a mixture because it contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases that are not chemically joined in a single formula. Sea water is also a mixture because sodium chloride is dissolved in water without forming one new compound. Mixtures can often be separated by physical methods. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a solution, and a magnet can separate magnetic iron filings from non-magnetic sulfur before heating. These methods do not split compounds into elements in the same simple way.

questions.question: Why is air a mixture?
questions.modelAnswer: Air contains several gases that are not chemically joined in one fixed formula.

questions.question: Which method separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
questions.modelAnswer: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.

questions.question: Which physical method can recover salt from salt water?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaporation can remove the water and leave salt behind.

questions.question: Why can a magnet separate iron filings from sulfur before heating?
questions.modelAnswer: Iron is magnetic and sulfur is not, and before heating they are mixed rather than chemically joined.

questions.question: Explain why physical separation methods are evidence that salt water is a mixture rather than a compound.
questions.modelAnswer: Salt water can be separated by evaporation because the salt and water are not chemically joined in one fixed compound.

data.sourcePassage: Chemical symbols are short codes for elements. The first letter is always capitalised, and if there is a second letter it is lower case. This matters because Co means cobalt, while CO means carbon and oxygen together in a formula. Cl means chlorine, but CL is not the correct symbol. A chemical formula shows which atoms are present and how many of each type are shown. If there is no small number after a symbol, it means one atom of that element. In CO2, C means one carbon atom and O2 means two oxygen atoms. In NH3, N means one nitrogen atom and H3 means three hydrogen atoms. A formula helps classify a substance, but it does not show colour, safety, exact size or full shape.

questions.question: Which is the correct symbol for chlorine?
questions.modelAnswer: Cl is the correct symbol for chlorine.

questions.question: What is the difference between Co and CO?
questions.modelAnswer: Co is cobalt, while CO means carbon and oxygen together in a formula.

questions.question: What does CO2 show?
questions.modelAnswer: CO2 shows one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.

questions.question: How many nitrogen and hydrogen atoms are shown in NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: NH3 shows one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: Why should a student not use a formula to decide the colour or safety of a substance?
questions.modelAnswer: A formula shows atom types and numbers, not visible properties, safety, exact size or full shape.

data.sourcePassage: The periodic table arranges elements in a pattern. Each element has its own place, and an element tile usually shows the element name, chemical symbol and atomic number. Columns are called groups, and elements in the same group often have similar properties. Rows are called periods. Metals are mostly found on the left and in the centre of the table, while non-metals are mostly found on the right. The source extract shows hydrogen, lithium and sodium in group 1, and helium, neon and argon in group 18. Helium, neon and argon are unreactive gases. It also shows carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon in period 2. Hydrogen is a non-metal, even though it is often placed on the left because of the layout of the table.

questions.modelAnswer: It usually shows the element name, chemical symbol and atomic number.

questions.question: What is a group in the periodic table?
questions.modelAnswer: A group is a column in the periodic table.

questions.question: Which group contains helium, neon and argon in the source extract?
questions.modelAnswer: Helium, neon and argon are shown in group 18.

questions.question: Where are metals mostly found in the periodic table?
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are mostly on the left and in the centre of the periodic table.

questions.question: Why can hydrogen be confusing when using the periodic table layout?

data.sourcePassage: Heating iron and sulfur is a useful case study for distinguishing a mixture from a compound. Before heating, grey iron filings and yellow sulfur powder are together but not chemically joined. A magnet attracts the iron, showing that iron still keeps its magnetic property. During strong heating, the mixture glows and becomes very hot. After heating, a black solid forms. The black solid is iron sulfide, a compound with properties different from iron and sulfur. It cannot be separated with a magnet in the same simple way. The observations provide evidence for a chemical reaction: a new substance formed and the properties changed. A good conclusion links observations to an explanation, rather than just repeating what was seen.

questions.modelAnswer: A black solid forms after heating.

questions.question: What is the name of the compound formed from iron and sulfur?
questions.modelAnswer: Iron sulfide forms.

questions.question: What evidence shows that iron kept its own property before heating?
questions.modelAnswer: A magnet attracted the iron filings before heating.

questions.modelAnswer: It is a new substance with different properties from the starting iron and sulfur.

questions.question: What should a strong conclusion include for this practical?
questions.modelAnswer: It should link observations, such as the black solid and changed magnetic behaviour, to the explanation that iron sulfide formed.
